strengths: Well-motivated identification of a real and underexplored bottleneck (fine-grained perception vs. reasoning) in MLLMs' abstract visual reasoning, supported by a clean, convincing ablation (Table 4) replacing raw images with perceptual descriptions that produces large accuracy jumps for both GPT-4o and Qwen2.5VL.

VisuRiddles benchmark is carefully constructed with a structured Collection-Cleaning-Consolidation pipeline, human quality control (12 annotators), and covers 5 core dimensions plus 2 high-level reasoning categories (RAVEN, Sudoku) with free-form/constraint-based answers that mitigate guessing.

The Perceptual Riddle Synthesizer (PRS) provides scalable automated data synthesis with paired fine-grained perceptual JSON annotations, enabling intermediate supervision rather than only QA pairs; ablation on data scale (Table 5) shows consistent monotonic gains with more synthetic data.

Broad evaluation of 17 MLLMs (open-source and proprietary, including thinking-mode and CoT variants) shows that most models perform near random chance, and that scaling model size or applying CoT/inference-time scaling does not meaningfully help, reinforcing the paper's core claim.

Fine-tuning a 7B model (Qwen2.5-VL-7B) on PRS-generated data yields large improvements (20.9 -> 43.7 average), including dramatic gains on high-level tasks (Sudoku 0->60, RAVEN 14->95), providing reasonably strong evidence for the practical utility of the synthesis framework.
Qualitative case studies (Fig. 4) illustrate concrete failure modes of thinking-mode and CoT approaches versus the perception-enhanced model, adding interpretability to the quantitative results.
weaknesses: The benchmark is relatively small (1000 questions total, with only 100 each for the two high-level categories), which may lead to noisy per-category accuracy estimates, especially for Sudoku/RAVEN with only 100 samples each.

The near-perfect gains on RAVEN/Sudoku after PRS fine-tuning (0->60/95) could partly reflect distributional overlap or format similarity between PRS-synthesized RAVEN/Sudoku training data and the benchmark's RAVEN/Sudoku test items (both use similar generation methods/protocols), raising concerns about data leakage or overfitting to synthetic task formats rather than genuine perceptual generalization; this is not carefully disentangled.

There is no comparison against other data synthesis or CoT-supervision baselines beyond the model's own baseline and general MLLMs; e.g., it is unclear how PRS compares to simply fine-tuning on QA pairs without perceptual descriptions (an ablation isolating the effect of perceptual descriptions vs. just having more in-domain synthetic AVR training data would strengthen the central claim).

The 'Other' category consistently degrades with more PRS training data (Table 5), which is not adequately explained or analyzed, raising questions about generalization outside the specific rule types covered by PRS.

Details on PRS generation are somewhat abstract (e.g., exact procedure for auto-generating icons, ensuring rule-answer uniqueness, controlling difficulty) and reproducibility could be limited without the promised code/dataset release; no release was confirmed at submission time.

Human performance baseline (via Fenbi platform, presumably answer keys/expert stats rather than actual live human test-takers) is unclear in how it was measured (e.g., sample size, time constraints), casting some uncertainty on the human accuracy comparison used prominently in the introduction.
Statistical significance and variance of results (e.g., single run vs averaged) are not reported, and the paper largely relies on single-run absolute numbers to argue for large qualitative claims.

The related work and framing rely on a large number of loosely characterized benchmarks/methods without deeply engaging in comparisons of VisuRiddles' specific advantages/disadvantages relative to closely related AVR-focused datasets (e.g., ConceptARC, PGM, RAVEN variants) beyond generic claims of 'broader dimension coverage.'

strengths: Introduces a benchmark (VisuRiddles) that spans multiple cognitively-motivated dimensions (numerosity/attribute/style/position/spatiality) plus two higher-level tasks (RAVEN, Sudoku), which is a reasonable attempt to go beyond single-dimension AVR benchmarks.

The visual-vs-perceptual-description ablation (Table 4) is a clean and fairly convincing demonstration that providing explicit structured descriptions of the abstract graphics substantially improves model accuracy, supporting the paper's central claim.
Broad empirical coverage: 17 MLLMs (open-source and proprietary, with and without 'thinking'/CoT modes) are evaluated, giving a reasonably comprehensive picture of current model limitations on AVR.

The PRS synthetic data generation pipeline with rule/sub-rule decomposition and rendered perceptual JSON annotations is a sensible engineering approach to producing intermediate supervision signals, and the ablation over data scale (Table 5) shows a generally monotonic trend.
Case studies (Fig. 4) are illustrative and help ground the quantitative claims in qualitative failure analysis.
weaknesses: The central finding—that providing textual/structured descriptions instead of raw images boosts performance—is close to tautological: handcrafted, near-ground-truth perceptual descriptions convert a vision problem into a text problem that LLMs are already strong at, which doesn't cleanly disentangle 'perception' from simply removing the visual modality altogether. This weakens the strength of the claimed insight, which is also not particularly novel (similar observations exist in prior visual-cognition-gap work cited by the paper itself, e.g. ref [2]).

The PRS training data is generated using the same rule categories (numerical, stylistic, attribute, positional, spatial, sudoku, RAVEN) as the VisuRiddles benchmark itself, so the large gains of PRS-Qwen2.5VL-7B are essentially in-distribution improvements on near-identical task formats rather than evidence of a generalizable perceptual capability. No external/standard AVR benchmarks (e.g., original RAVEN, PGM, ConceptARC, MathVista) are used to test whether the perceptual gains transfer beyond the paper's own synthetic/benchmark distribution.

PRS fine-tuning is only validated on a single backbone (Qwen2.5-VL-7B); no experiments show the approach generalizes across model families or scales, which is important given the paper's broad claims about 'current MLLMs'.

Benchmark size is modest (1000 total questions, with only 100 Sudoku and 100 RAVEN items) and several inconsistencies appear in the reported statistics (e.g., text states 770k/'770ok' samples in basic categories vs. Table 1 showing 800 basic + 200 high-level = 1000, and a seemingly erroneous '770ok' typo), raising concerns about the care taken in reporting and possibly in data curation.

The human performance baseline methodology is underspecified (sourced from the Fenbi platform but it is unclear how many human subjects, what their expertise level was, or how scores were aggregated), making the human vs. model comparison in Fig. 1(a) and Table 3 harder to interpret rigorously.

Potential data contamination is not addressed: the benchmark is built from publicly available Chinese Civil Service Exam questions (via the Fenbi platform), which may already appear in the pretraining corpora of large commercial models, confounding the 'low performance equals poor perception' narrative.

The 'Other' category consistently fails to improve (or even degrades slightly) with increasing PRS training data (Table 5), which is not discussed in depth and undermines the claim that fine-grained perceptual supervision uniformly helps.

No statistical significance testing, variance across runs, or confidence intervals are reported for any of the main results, despite fairly small category sample sizes (e.g., 69–156 items per dimension), making some reported differences of a few accuracy points difficult to interpret as meaningful.

Comparisons mix fundamentally different answer formats (single-choice 4-way vs. open-ended symbolic Sudoku/RAVEN outputs) into a single averaged 'Avg' metric, which can be misleading since large swings in a few high-level categories dominate the average.

strengths: Well-motivated and cognitively grounded framing: decomposing AVR into five core perceptual dimensions plus two high-level reasoning categories (RAVEN, Sudoku) gives a principled and interpretable benchmark structure rather than an arbitrary mix of tasks.

VisuRiddles benchmark construction is careful, with a documented Collection-Cleaning-Consolidation pipeline, multiple trained annotators, cross-validation, and human baseline scores collected from a real exam-prep platform, lending credibility to the benchmark quality.

The core claim (fine-grained perception, not reasoning, is the bottleneck) is supported by a direct and fairly convincing ablation (Table 4): replacing raw images with structured perceptual descriptions yields large, consistent accuracy jumps for both GPT-4o and Qwen2.5-VL-72B across nearly all task types, including a striking near-zero to 65% jump on Sudoku.

The Perceptual Riddle Synthesizer (PRS) is a sensible automated pipeline (rule selection, element configuration, rendering+annotation) that produces both diverse abstract graphics and aligned fine-grained perceptual descriptions, enabling intermediate supervision that most existing AVR datasets lack.

Data-scaling ablation (Table 5) shows a clean, monotonic improvement with increasing amounts of PRS-generated training data, which is a good sanity check that the gains are attributable to the training data itself rather than confounds.

Broad evaluation across 17 MLLMs (11 open-source, 6 proprietary, including 'thinking'-mode and CoT-prompted variants) gives a reasonably comprehensive picture of the current landscape and supports the finding that scaling and inference-time reasoning strategies alone do not close the gap to human performance.
weaknesses: The fine-tuned/perception-enhanced model is only demonstrated on a single base model (Qwen2.5-VL-7B); it is unclear whether PRS-based training generalizes to other architectures or scales (e.g., larger or differently-pretrained backbones), which limits the generality of the central claim that perceptual supervision is broadly transferable.

Benchmark scale for the high-level categories is small (100 RAVEN and 100 Sudoku items each), which may produce high-variance accuracy estimates, especially given results are reported to one decimal place; no confidence intervals or repeated-run variance are reported anywhere in the paper.

The 'Other' category is the one dimension where PRS training consistently hurts performance (Table 5), suggesting a domain/distribution mismatch between synthetic data and this category that is not discussed or analyzed in depth.

The perceptual-description ablation (Table 4) essentially removes the visual modality entirely by substituting text descriptions for images; while this supports the perception bottleneck hypothesis, it does not fully disentangle whether gains from PRS training on the main benchmark stem from improved visual perception per se versus the model learning to imitate the specific structured/verbose CoT-like format used in the synthetic descriptions.

Technical novelty of PRS itself is somewhat incremental: procedural/rule-based generation of matrix-style visual reasoning puzzles (RAVEN, PGM, I-RAVEN, etc.) is well established; the main new ingredient is pairing generation with fine-grained textual perceptual annotations, which, while useful, is a relatively straightforward extension.

Details on human evaluation (number of participants, expertise, whether they solved RAVEN/Sudoku items) are sparse, and no human baseline is reported for the two high-level reasoning categories in Table 3, leaving the human-vs-model gap only partially characterized.

There is a risk that some civil-service-exam-sourced benchmark questions could already be present in web-scale pretraining corpora of the evaluated proprietary models, and the paper does not discuss decontamination checks or the possibility of memorization affecting the reported near-random baseline performance.

The paper's writing has several typos/inconsistencies (e.g., '770ok samples', slightly garbled table/rule descriptions), which, while not affecting the core contribution, suggest the manuscript could benefit from additional proofreading before publication.

strengths: Identifies and convincingly demonstrates (via Table 3's visual vs. perceptual-description ablation) that fine-grained perception, rather than reasoning per se, is a primary bottleneck for MLLMs on abstract visual reasoning (AVR) tasks—an insight that is both intuitive and empirically well-supported.

Introduces a new benchmark (VisuRiddles) built from real-world civil service exam riddles with a documented collection/cleaning/consolidation pipeline involving twelve trained annotators, covering eight reasoning categories from basic perceptual dimensions to higher-level RAVEN/Sudoku reasoning.

Proposes a synthesizer that automatically generates AVR instances paired with structured perceptual descriptions and validated CoT solutions, addressing the real gap that existing AVR datasets lack intermediate perceptual annotations.

The two-stage SFT (perception) + RL/GRPO (reasoning) training paradigm (PAVR) yields large, consistent gains over the 7B baseline (24.6 → 46.8 average) and outperforms many larger open-source and commercial models, providing fairly convincing evidence for the paper's central claim.

Extensive experimental breadth: 17+ evaluated models (including recent commercial systems like GPT-5, Gemini-2.5-Pro, Qwen3-VL-235B), thorough ablations isolating the contributions of Caption/CoT/GRPO components, and a secondary validation on the external VisuLogic benchmark.
Useful qualitative case studies (Fig. 5) illustrating failure modes of inference-time scaling/CoT prompting versus PAVR's perception-grounded 'rethink' behavior.
weaknesses: Potential concern about the independence of training and evaluation distributions: the synthesizer used to generate SFT/RL training data is built from the same rule categories/patterns as the benchmark itself, raising questions about how much of PAVR's benchmark improvement reflects genuine generalizable reasoning gains versus stylistic/format matching to VisuRiddles-like data; the weaker relative performance on the external VisuLogic benchmark (PAVR not best among 38B RL models despite far fewer parameters) partially supports this concern and deserves more explicit discussion.

The CoT annotations used for SFT/GRPO are generated by prompting a commercial model (Gemini-2.5-Flash-Think) with perceptual descriptions and keeping only examples with correct final answers; this validation only checks answer correctness, not reasoning faithfulness, so flawed or spurious reasoning chains could still be included and propagated into the trained model.

Benchmark scale is relatively modest (1,000 total instances, with high-level categories like Sudoku/RAVEN comprising only 100 each), which may limit the statistical robustness of fine-grained category-level comparisons.

Uniform near-zero scores for many models on Sudoku (constraint-based exact-match) suggest the evaluation protocol may be overly strict or brittle, making it hard to distinguish genuine reasoning failure from formatting/output-parsing issues.

Methodological details of the human baseline (population, sample size, testing conditions via the Fenbi platform) are not clearly described, making it hard to assess comparability with model evaluations.
Some writing/grammar issues throughout (e.g., 'It unexpected that...', 'a innovative and comprehensive resource') reduce overall polish.

Authors acknowledge the icon library and rule pool used for synthesis are limited in scale/diversity, which may constrain the generality of the perceptual descriptions and downstream training benefits.

strengths: Introduces a new benchmark (VisuRiddles) spanning 5 basic perceptual categories plus 2 high-level reasoning tasks (RAVEN-style, Sudoku), sourced from real civil-service exam riddles, with a documented collection/cleaning/consolidation pipeline.

Proposes an automatic synthesizer that pairs abstract graphics with structured perceptual descriptions and CoT solutions, addressing the lack of intermediate perceptual annotations in prior AVR datasets.

Extensive evaluation of 17+ open-source and commercial MLLMs (including very recent models such as GPT-5, Qwen3-VL, Gemini-2.5-Pro), giving a reasonably broad empirical picture of current model performance on AVR.
The perception-vs-reasoning ablation (feeding structured text descriptions instead of raw images) is an intuitive and illustrative experiment that supports the paper's central narrative.
Two-stage SFT+GRPO training pipeline yields large, consistent gains over the 7B baseline on the in-domain VisuRiddles benchmark across all categories.
weaknesses: The central claim that 'perception is the primary bottleneck' is not particularly novel; it echoes several already-cited works (e.g., MMVP/'Eyes Wide Shut', MARVEL, VisuLogic) that have made closely related observations about perceptual shortcomings of MLLMs in abstract/structured visual tasks.

Generalization claims are not well supported: on the external VisuLogic benchmark, PAVR (30.6 overall) is actually *lower* than InternVL2.5-38B-RL (31.1) trained specifically on VisuLogic data, and only marginally ahead of other baselines, which undercuts the paper's claim that PAVR 'substantially outperforms' other models and that the approach generalizes beyond the training distribution/taxonomy.

Strong overlap between the synthesizer's rule taxonomy (Numerical/Stylistic/Attribute/Positional/Spatial) and the benchmark's own category taxonomy raises concerns about distributional matching/overfitting to the specific question format and category structure of VisuRiddles rather than genuine improvement in perceptual or reasoning ability; no held-out category or cross-taxonomy generalization test is provided within VisuRiddles itself.

The 'real-world' framing of the benchmark is inconsistent: the two high-level categories (RAVEN, Sudoku) are explicitly noted to be synthetically generated rather than collected from real riddles, which is not clearly flagged in the main text claims about the benchmark being 'collected from real-world data.'

No verification is provided that the structured perceptual descriptions used in the ablation (Table 3) and for SFT are not simply making the task textually solvable without real visual grounding (i.e., risk that gains reflect benefiting from an easier text-based proxy task rather than evidence about visual perception per se).

Benchmark scale is modest (1000 total questions, several sub-categories <100 samples), limiting statistical reliability of per-category comparisons, and no variance/multiple-run analysis is reported for any model.

Unclear exact correspondence between the method description in Sec. 4 (SFT with 'structured perceptual descriptions') and the ablation table terminology ('Caption' vs 'CoT' vs 'PAVR-SFT'), making it hard to verify precisely what training data/supervision produces the reported 39.5 SFT result.

No comparison against other recent AVR-specific training approaches (e.g., VisualSphinx, Visual-RFT, VisualPRM) as baselines trained under comparable conditions, despite citing them as related work; this makes it hard to assess whether the proposed two-stage pipeline is actually superior to existing training recipes rather than just to untrained baselines.

Potential benchmark contamination is not discussed: items drawn from a public, widely-used Chinese civil-service exam preparation platform could plausibly appear in the pretraining corpora of large commercial models, which is not addressed.

Writing contains several grammatical errors and unclear phrasing (e.g., 'a innovative', 'It unexpected that models...'), and some figures/tables (e.g., exact-match criterion for Sudoku grid predictions) lack sufficient methodological detail.

strengths: Identifies and empirically supports an interesting and underexplored hypothesis: that fine-grained perception, rather than reasoning per se, is the primary bottleneck limiting MLLM performance on Abstract Visual Reasoning (AVR) tasks.

Introduces a genuinely useful resource combination: a benchmark curated from real-world (civil service exam) riddles with careful multi-annotator cleaning, spanning 5 basic perceptual dimensions plus 2 high-level reasoning tasks (RAVEN, Sudoku), providing broader and more systematic coverage than many prior AVR benchmarks.

The VisuRiddles Synthesizer is a thoughtful design that automatically pairs abstract graphics with structured perceptual descriptions and CoT solutions, addressing a real gap (lack of perceptual annotations) in existing AVR training data.

Strong empirical results: the 7B PAVR model, trained via the proposed SFT+GRPO pipeline, substantially outperforms much larger open-source models (up to 671B) and commercial models (GPT-5, Gemini-2.5-Pro, Claude-3.7) on the proposed benchmark.

Well-designed ablations (Table 3 raw-image vs. perceptual-description input; Table 4 Caption/CoT/GRPO components) that directly support the central claim by isolating the contribution of perception from reasoning enhancements.
Broad evaluation coverage (17 models, including several with 'thinking' modes and CoT prompting) and an additional out-of-domain evaluation on the VisuLogic benchmark to test generalization.
Illustrative case studies (Fig. 1, Fig. 4, Fig. 5) that make the perception-vs-reasoning distinction intuitive and support the quantitative findings qualitatively.
weaknesses: The central 'perception is the bottleneck' claim relies heavily on comparing raw-image input vs. hand-crafted textual perceptual descriptions (Table 3); this setup conflates 'perception' with 'multimodal-to-text conversion quality' and doesn't fully rule out that MLLMs are simply better at reasoning over clean text than over vision-language joint representations, which is a related but distinct issue from perceptual acuity.

Potential data leakage/overlap risk: the benchmark's real-world problems and the synthesizer's 'rule pool' are both derived from similar sources (civil service exams / standardized tests), raising concern that the synthesized training rules may closely mirror benchmark rule structures, inflating in-domain gains relative to genuine generalization.

Generalization to the out-of-domain VisuLogic benchmark (Table 7) is much more modest — PAVR (7B) is only roughly on par with or slightly below a considerably different 38B RL-tuned baseline, suggesting the large VisuRiddles gains may partly reflect distribution matching to the synthesizer's rule types rather than broad AVR competence.

The rule pool and icon gallery used by the synthesizer are relatively limited and hand-designed (as acknowledged in the Limitations), which may cap the diversity of reasoning patterns the model can learn and could bias evaluation toward rule types well-represented in the synthetic data.

Missing statistical robustness details: no variance/error bars, no discussion of benchmark answer leakage checks for large commercial models, and limited hyperparameter/reward details for the GRPO stage.

Even the best model (PAVR) remains well below human performance across most categories, and the paper does not deeply analyze remaining failure modes beyond the illustrative single case study in Fig. 5.

The RL component (GRPO with simple answer/format rewards) is a fairly standard adoption of DeepSeek-R1-style training rather than a novel methodological contribution, so the technical novelty is concentrated mainly in the benchmark/synthesizer rather than the training algorithm.
Minor writing/clarity issues throughout (e.g., grammatical errors, some overly dense explanations of the synthesis pipeline) that could be improved for readability.
